evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 《說文》; 金文; historical uses
evidence.text: The entry says the bronze form is composed of 水 plus phonetic 曷 and denotes water drying up; it reports 渴 used for 竭 in the Warring States Zhongshan King Fanghu inscription, and quotes the Shuowen gloss 盡也 (“exhausted”). It separately records dryness/parching, thirst in 詩·王風·君子于役, and urgent in 公羊傳·隱公三年. Its Mawangdui Laozi example is a Han manuscript reading 渴 for 竭. The source displays bronze, seal, and manuscript examples; its page shows no oracle-bone example. These are the database’s paleographic and lexicographic assertions, not visual inspection of the glyph images.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 渴

evidence.text: The transcribed Fanghu text includes 賙竭志盡忠, where the CUHK entry identifies the bronze graph 渴 as a writing of 竭. The page dates the Zhongshan King vessels to the king’s fourteenth year, approximately 314 BCE. The current transcription prints 竭 and does not itself reproduce or photographically establish the precise graph shape in the inscription.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The entry cites 詩·王風·君子于役 (“苟無飢渴”) for thirst, 公羊傳·隱公三年 (“渴葬”) for urgency, and Tang poet Bai Juyi for dryness/parching. It thereby documents distinct older usages but does not establish a precise date for the earliest surviving manuscript of the poem or commentary.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 渴

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The entry quotes Xu Shen’s Eastern Han-era Shuowen: 渴, 盡也, 从水，曷聲, with fanqie 苦葛切. It also lists Guangyun fanqie 苦曷 and 渠列 and the corresponding Middle Chinese categories: 溪, 入聲, 山攝寒/曷開一 and 群, 入聲, 山攝仙/薛開三. Shuowen is evidence for an early Han lexicographic analysis, not independent proof of the graph’s prehistoric origin.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 渴

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The 曷 entry quotes 《說文》: 何也，从曰，匃聲, fanqie 胡葛切; it lists Middle Chinese 匣母, 入聲, 山攝寒/曷開一. The same database groups 曷 and 渴 among Cantonese homophones, supporting a historical sound-component analysis at its level of phonological description. Its account says the interior element in the bronze 曷 form is unclear, cautioning against a confident reconstruction of that component’s original referent.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 曷

evidence.field: sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv row 1886; pipeline/data/unihan-kmandarin-hsk1.tsv row 252; kMandarin; official character record
evidence.text: Local rows checked: 渴 is Mandarin kě; Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *Nə-[k]ʰˤat (Middle Chinese khat), gloss “thirsty,” GSR 0313j. 曷 is Mandarin hé; Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *[g]ˤat, gloss “what,” GSR 0313d. These are the local dataset’s exact notations. They indicate a plausible rhyme/coda correspondence but different initials in this reconstruction; they do not erase the traditional phonetic-component analysis. Current Unihan Mandarin metadata is not evidence for ancient phonology. The official per-character lookup URL was attempted but was inaccessible in the web tool; the searchable Unicode chart confirms the Unihan service, not the exact character-specific rows.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The account presents 渴 as an old graph used for the word later written 竭 in the sense ‘exhausted/dried up’; it does not describe 曷 as a whole graph borrowed to write 渴. Rather, 曷 is analyzed as the phonetic element inside 渴. The transition from that older ‘dry up/exhaust’ usage to ‘thirsty’ is semantically plausible, and the source records both uses, but does not document the exact bridging stages or dates for the shift. It also says later semantic functions were redistributed among 喝, 渴, and 竭.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 渴

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The source quotes Shuowen’s analysis of 曷 as 从曰、匃聲 and states that its bronze form has two 口 elements while the middle portion is unclear. Thus the source supplies no secure original depicted referent for that ancient shape. That uncertainty does not undermine its separate attested readings or 曷’s phonetic role in 渴.

gaps: The exact official Unicode per-character pages for 渴 (U+6E34) and 曷 (U+66F7) could not be opened in the web tool. Local exact rows were checked: pipeline/data/unihan-kmandarin-hsk1.tsv row 252 lists 渴 kMandarin kě; row 215 lists 曷 kMandarin hé. Local Baxter–Sagart rows 1886 and 1245 were checked. No verified character-specific upstream HTTP page for those exact Unihan values was obtained.

The CUHK page lists graphic examples but this research did not inspect the glyph images visually. It does not list a 渴 oracle-bone form; no claim is made that the graph is absent from all oracle-bone corpora.

The early bronze reading as 竭 and meaning ‘water dried up/exhausted’ are attributed to the CUHK database. The opened inscription transcription renders the phrase with 竭, so it does not independently show the specific graphic form 渴.

The semantic development from ‘exhausted/dried up’ to ‘thirsty/parched’ is not traced through dated intermediate attestations here. The Shijing citation is an early textual use, but its earliest surviving physical witness and exact date were not established.

Shuowen gives an Eastern Han lexicographic explanation; it is not direct evidence for the earliest formation of 渴. The bronze graph’s 曷 element has an uncertain middle referent, but this does not negate its independently supported phonetic role.

No local or external evidence inspected establishes a positional/full-form or chronological relationship between 氵 and 水 beyond the ordinary component analysis, so no separate origin_form claim is assigned here.

No small versioned local extract is recommended: the recurring database’s reuse terms for its character-specific scholarly material were not verified, so permission and editorial value for tracking extracted source text are not both established.
